subsubtopic: FINANCING OF ENERGY PROJECT IN SOVIET UNION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Government of Canada has finally found over $600 million to loan to people in dire straits. The Export Development Corporation is entering into an agreement with the Soviet Union to help finance a huge sour gas megaproject at Astrakhan. The EDC is providing loan financing of $637.5 million at the unconscionable rate of 10 per cent. This means that the project will be interest subsidized, by Canadian people, to the amount of $198.5 million. Therefore 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer):
That at a time when Amoco and Chevron have pulled out of our own Alsands project, and when our major NATO allies have levied trade sanctions against the Soviet Union for its military imperialism, this House recommends an immediate review of this deal with the Communists by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and that the terms of the so-called "Friendship Treaty" signed in the early seventies between Canada and Russia be likewise reviewed.

speechtext:

with our NATO allies to impose meaningful sanctions against the present regime in Poland.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. It arises out of the announcement yesterday that Amoco and Chevron are withdrawing from the Alsands consortium. In April of 1980 this project was all ready to go, needing only government approval. Some 20 months later, after a national energy policy promising self-sufficiency by 1990, this project which is so vital to self-sufficiency is falling apart. Yet, according to press reports, the minister is neither surprised nor concerned.
Will the minister explain to the House whether this withdrawal of Amoco and Chevron is part of some grand plan, and can he explain this plan to the House? If not, could he tell the House what he is doing to get this project back on track and under way as soon as possible?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the last few weeks there have been discussions between the government of Alberta, the Government of Canada, and the partners in the Alsands project. The two governments have put forward an offer which we find fair and sufficient. However, it was recognized at the time of those discussions that obviously both governments could not necessarily make an offer that would meet the demands of the weakest partner in such a consortium.
We were trying to put forward an offer that would be satisfactory for the whole project. There is a limit to how much

February 2, 1982
Oral Questions
the Canadian people should be asked to pay for this particular project. In that sense we are not surprised that those two companies have decided to withdraw from the consortium, and we are confident that the consortium will proceed, either through enlarged participation by the existing partners, or through new partners joining the consortium.
These discussions will carry on. It is my understanding that the consortium is supposed to meet shortly and review the situation among the remaining partners. We will see what they decide.

Madam Speaker, this project is not only vital to self-sufficiency, it is absolutely vital to Canada's economic development. Indeed, the Economic Council of Canada described the energy megaprojects as the only good thing the Canadian economy has going for it in the 1980s.
This two-year delay has already cost Canada untold billions of dollars and untold thousands of jobs. Sponsors indicate that unless an affirmative decision to go ahead is given by April they will have lost another construction season, another full year's delay.
In the interests of the billions of dollars that are being lost, and in the interests of the thousands of jobs which could be created by this project, will the Minister not commit to the House his assurance that this project will get under way as soon as possible so that another year is not lost while people walk the unemployment lines?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, both the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada have agreed on a proposal that we found fair.

Some protection.
Madam Speaker, who in the government is concerned about the thousands of Canadians who are unemployed because this project is delayed and held up?
Hear, hear!

Who in the government is concerned about the billions of dollars being lost? It is all well and good for the minister to stand in his place and say that he has to assure the people of Canada that he is doing the best job possible. The fact of the matter is that the people putting up the money are withdrawing, and this is costing the Canadian economy in general, and manufacturing and construction in particular, a fortune. It is affecting our balance of payments and interest rates.
Will the minister not make a commitment to the House to ensure that this vital project goes ahead? If he does not, we must start examining ways in which we will be able to control the social unrest in this country which will have a million unemployed throughout the entire 1980s?

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the same minister. I suggest that there are also limits to what a government can do to an investing company in Canada.
The minister must surely realize that one of the reasons Amoco and Chevron have withdrawn from the Alsands consortium is the treatment by this government of Syncrude, Suncor, and the oil industry in general, with its national energy policy, broken promises, and retroactivity. He must realize that investor confidence in Canada is at an all-time low.
What assurance has the minister given to the Arabs and the French that this government can be trusted not to treat their investment in Canada any differently from the way it has treated other investment in the energy sector in Canada?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, there are clear rules in this country in relation to foreign investment, particularly in the energy field. subtopic: EL SALVADOR-EFFECT OF TERRORISM ON POSSIBILITY OF HOLDING DEMOCRATIC ELECTIONS
EL SALVADOR-EFFECT OF TERRORISM ON POSSIBILITY OF HOLDING DEMOCRATIC ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and concerns the government's stated commitment to the view that democratic elections in El Salvador are now possible. The question arises from news at the weekend that government troops went into a suburb of San Salvador and murdered some 20 youths as a demonstration of terrorist tactics. Amongst the youths were a number of pre-adolescents.
Considering this most recent barbaric act, and considering that all-party delegations from Canada's parliament that have looked into the situation do not believe that democratic elections are possible in this circumstance, is the minister now prepared to change government policy and acknowledge that terrorism is no foundation for democratic elections and that peaceful negotiations, leading to the abolition of violence, are an essential condition at this time, before elections?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EL SALVADOR-EFFECT OF TERRORISM ON POSSIBILITY OF HOLDING DEMOCRATIC ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, these were terrible events that took place over the weekend in El Salvador. We condemn them, as we have condemned all such events. We have asked the government of El Salvador for an explanation. As the hon. member knows, there was some dispute about the facts. We would like to ascertain who is responsible. The events speak for themselves; they are too horrible to contemplate.
With respect to the question of elections in El Salvador, if we are speaking in the ideal, and we certainly would prefer to do so, as would the hon. member, we would want to see much better conditions for elections in El Salvador. In fact, through our initiative we tried to change the conditions that prevail in that country. We were turned down by the rebel forces very clearly in their response, and somewhat more ambiguously by the government which said the rebels would not accept it so it would not work. In any event, we did not succeed in changing the course of events in that country. We are seriously considering whether, in the circumstances, we should in any way participate in the election campaign in that country through observers or in any other fashion.

speechtext:

It is the junta that is turning down negotiations, not the so-called rebel forces.
I should like to ask a related question. Yesterday we learned that the United States government has made a decision to increase its military involvement in El Salvador rather signifi-

cantly. This can have no other effect than to further prop up the junta which was responsible for the murders on the weekend. Just the other day I received a copy of a letter from the Prime Minister in which he said, and 1 quote:
On the supply of arms to Guatemala and El Salvador . .. we have frequently expressed our opposition and have done so vigorously . . .
On behalf of the vast majority of Canadians who want to see a peaceful solution to the terrible situation in El Salvador, will the minister now implement what the prime minister committed himself to, and condemn the recent increase in the supply of arms by the United States to El Salvador?

subsubtopic: McDOUGALL REPORT ON CONDITIONS IN FOREIGN SERVICE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Prime Minister appointed Miss McDou-gall to do a study of our foreign service because of the dissatisfaction prevalent in it. Last December her report was made public. She found a crisis of identity, of confidence, in the ranks of the foreign service that required positive counteraction. She found a profound malaise and a communication gap between posts and headquarters, and a failure of management.
To date neither the Prime Minister nor the Secretary of State for External Affairs have made any statement on the report, even when the Prime Minister announced the reorganization of January 12. What is the response of the government to these startling findings? What action will be taken to carry out the recommendations? Will the foreign service be restored to proper management? Will its personnel be given the conditions under which they can perform to their capabilities? This
is the service for which the minister is responsible. What is he doing about this devastating indictment of the management of External Affairs?

subsubtopic: McDOUGALL REPORT ON CONDITIONS IN FOREIGN SERVICE-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister said that there was dissatisfaction in the ranks of the foreign service, and Miss McDougall confirmed it. The minister's department is reported to suffer from a failure of management and these people are characterized as demoralized, mistrustful and frustrated. This is the minister's department, not the Prime Minister's department.
The minister is responsible day by day for this department. When will the minister act to change these findings? Will he agree that this report be referred to the House of Commons Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence as Miss McDougall recommended, so that we can monitor his progress in carrying out the recommendations? Does he agree with that? Will he give our External Affairs people a chance to perform as they have the ability to perform, given proper leadership and management? When will he do that? When will he take this indictment seriously? Never mind the Prime Minister; if he is too busy to do anything, the minister must do it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. According to recent reports in La Presse and The Globe and Mail, the cabinet's economic development committee has been the green light to yet another massive bailout to Canada's nuclear industry. This bailout involves massive financing subsidies for potential foreign buyers. It will also involve a subsidy program here in Canada designed to entice the provinces into building reactors to export electricity to the United States.
The February 1 deadline for bids on the Mexican reactor deal has now passed, and whatever our offer to the Mexicans happens to be, it must have been tendered. At a time when Canadians are being asked to spend 20 per cent on mortgages, does our sales pitch include concessional financing at or near 7.5 per cent to 8 per cent as our competitors are bidding on the same reactor deal?
Flon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources): Madam Speaker, first of all I would like to assure the hon. member that the figures he is mentioning at best are very much hypothetical. We do not know what our competitors are proposing as concessional financing. We do not intend to tell our competitors what our offer is. This is a competition with several other countries in order to get the contract that will create several tens of thousands of jobs and, man-years for Canadians, over the next few years. This is a very important contract. It means jobs for Canadians. We intend to try to meet the competition. The exact financing arrangements will be known if and when Canada gets the contract in question.
As far as the particular concessional financing is concerned, I remind my hon. friend that there is a general rule for exports from Canada of all kinds of products ranging from automobiles to locomotives and various other kinds of manufactured products. In order to ensure that Canadians are going to sell goods abroad and create jobs in this country, we have to make arrangements to meet the competition. There is nothing special with Candu reactors compared to any other product that we are selling abroad. Our job is to sell Canadian goods abroad and we are going to take the means to do it.

Madam Speaker, it is very interesting that every time a question relating to the nuclear industry is raised it is always shrouded in secrecy. The public has a right to know about the billions we have already spent and the billions we intend to give away to foreign competitors on what I call the nuclear-electrical lunacy in which we are involved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to continue my speech on Bill C-88, which I was not able to conclude when we adjourned at ten o'clock last night, dealing with changes to the Farm Credit Corporation.
Last year, for example, the Farm Credit Corporation received $12 million in capital and could therefore borrow and lend out some $300 million. This present bill would raise the authorized capital of the Farm Credit Corporation by $75 million, but on the basis of past experience, the corporation can expect to get only about $12 million to $15 million of that in the coming year; that is, enough to allow it to borrow and re-lend from $300 million to $375 million. This is far short of what farmers need now and in the coming year, but it is also far short of what this legislation seems in theory to be making available.
It would be a great advantage if the government were to concentrate its efforts on helping the Farm Credit Corporation get ready to borrow privately, so that the government could grant more of the authorized capital in the coming year and do less of the authorized lending. One solution is precisely the plan the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is now toying with, namely, allowing retiring farmers to place their money with the Farm Credit Corporation at low rates and avoid tax of the type introduced in the November budget which is designed in such a way as to cripple the retirement plans which many have been making for the last few years. All of this could and should be discussed in committee. What is important is to see that the Farm Credit Corporation is helped to utilize the new capital authorization now being proposed for it, rather than hindered by the government, as it has been in recent years.
There are other features of this legislation which appear to be of a routine nature and which seem welcome on the surface. One such feature is a loosening of the definition of farming which should allow the corporation more flexibility in dealing with the changing face of Canadian agriculture and husbandry, rather than tying it to models from the past. The dropping of present age restrictions is another feature which seems welcome, and certainly it is in line with the will of the House as expressed in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which we so recently adopted. It is to be hoped that the Farm Credit Corporation will adopt this change, not only in form but also in spirit. There are other changes in this bill which are of a more technical nature, such as changes in the size of the board and its quorum, and turning over some matters to regulations,
Farm Loans
which should prove worthwhile, but which should certainly receive some scrutiny from the committee as it examines this bill.
One of the main problems which will have to be confronted in effecting this legislation is the problem of ensuring that the Farm Credit Corporation can borrow private funds at a low enough rate to allow it to lend at an acceptable rate. In this connection, it is interesting to note recent press reports indicating that the Farm Credit Corporation has been approached with an offer of private money at rates much lower than the prevailing commercial lending rates in Canada. According to the press reports, however, the Farm Credit Corporation does not know the source of the funds being offered. Speculation, therefore, suggests various possibilities, including the possibility that the funds being offered are from illegal sources, such as the proceeds from the international drug trade or other organized crime activities. Rather than see the Farm Credit Corporation accept money from such anonymous sources, perhaps the Minister of Agriculture will prevail upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to adopt the suggestion he aired last week, that retiring farmers might have their own kind of registered retirement savings plan by lending to the Farm Credit Corporation at reduced rates and with a corresponding tax reduction. This is not any sort of obnoxious tax expenditure on the part of the government, as the Minister of Finance seems to think all money is when other people have it, but, rather, a recognition that the capitalization of agriculture, if we are to see the survival of the family farm in Canada, is a special case, just as the non-taxation of capital gains on a principal residence is a special case associated with the socially desirable goal of seeing people own their own houses.
Certainly there is no advantage in allowing the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow privately if it must borrow at the outrageously high rates caused by the government's high interest rate policy. There must be a means worked out whereby the Farm Credit Corporation is not entirely dependent on the public treasury for its borrowing, yet can borrow at a low enough rate that its clients, Canada's food producers, can afford to reborrow from it at manageable rates. This, it seems to me, is an issue which must be faced and which the committee examination must deal with squarely.
There are other matters which I was hoping to see in this bill, Mr. Speaker, but which are not mentioned at all. For example, up until now there have been many cases where the Farm Credit Corporation has refused to treat the spouses of farmers as they would treat other partners in assessing loan applications, even though in a great many cases both spouses work full time or what many industrial workers would consider to be much more than full time. I asked the head of the Farm Credit Corporation about this last spring, and I would like to remind the House of his response. He said:
We are preparing right now to send a demand-and this is a decision of the cabinet for regulation-to abolish entirely this regulation we have right now.
In other words, the Farm Credit Corporation seems prepared to treat men and women equally in this matter, as partners. Apparently the government is not, for we find no

February 2, 1982
Farm Loans
proposed change here, even though we in all parties supported the granting of equality to both men and women when we recently voted on the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It is interesting to recall how slow the cabinet was to accept that principle of equality, and now to see that they have not acted to give it legislative effect in this case now before us.
Another matter which I would have liked to see addressed is foreign takeovers of Canadian farms with Farm Credit Corporation mortgages. We live in a riding in western Ontario, and we know that a large percentage of our prime agricultural lands are being purchased, not only by foreign buyers, but also by absentee buyers. We know that we cannot compete with some of the rates which are being offered for some of the foreign money which is being brought into this country. We know that we are competing against money which has been earned in industrial areas of other countries. We would like to see people come to this country to set up residency, taking their place beside us, if they want to be producers of agricultural products. However, it is a different matter when foreigners buy our prime lands, very often leasing those lands out to the farmers who have farmed those lands for a number of years with as low as a 5 per cent return on their investment. There is simply no possible way that our young farmers, even with the help of the Farm Credit Corporation, can handle such purchases or compete against this type of buyer.
When selling farms, we want to be able to sell to the highest bidder. This is one area that should be addressed. 1 realize that jurisdiction over property is a provincial matter. However, I would feel bad if we did not include in this bill something to restrict FCC capital being used to facilitate a foreign purchaser who has no intention of residing in this country.
Last spring I asked the chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation about this matter. I quote from his answer at that time:
Right now the act says that we can incorporate in the mortgage a covenant saying that our borrower will not sell his farm without our permission. However, in the act as it is, it does not say that if he does not do that we can call the loan. It seems to be the logical thing to do, but it does not say it in the act.
When we were contemplating making amendments to our act this is one of the amendments that we wished to bring in, stating that in the case where he does that without our permission we can call in the loan. That would be one correction.
Right now, we have an internal policy by which we will not accept an assumption if the chap is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident. We will also refuse persons related to the business of real estate; we will refuse companies who do not meet our criteria for being principally occupied in agriculture; and finally, examine all cases where the person involved will not use the property for farming purposes.
This is as far as we have gone recently in the administration of that. We are getting ready to publish an internal policy on this .... The trouble with a policy of that sort is that we never know if it will stand up in court. In certain provinces, it would be pretty hard because of provincial legislation. However, so far, all the cases we have refused have not been challenged; so we still do not know.
It is my hope and intention when this bill goes to committee to introduce an amendment to include recognition of the spouse as a partner in a farming operation and to introduce an
amendment pertaining to the transfer of Farm Credit Corporation mortgages to non-residents of Canada.
Here is an area where farm credit is expected to see some legislative action. In examining this bill in committee we will want to know how far it goes toward giving adequate legislative backing to the policy. If there is any danger of a challenge to the policy in court, let us be clear in giving a legislative answer so that the courts will have certainty in denying such challenges.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak on Bill C-88 this afternoon. The constituency of Dauphin is a farming community. The farmers are not only involved in livestock and grain, but a very large number are involved in mixed farming. Of course, the family farm is still a reality for many people in my constituency. Farming is carried on in most parts of my constituency, in the north, Swan River Valley, around Dauphin, in the south, and the east in my constituency in the Alonsa, Plumas, or Amaranth area. There is a large area of potential for grain marketing and grain development. Because there is this large number of people in my constituency who are affected by this bill, I am pleased to speak on it this afternoon.
I am interested in the fact that there is mention of changes for Indian bands involved in farming. Of the seven Indian reserves in my constituency, a couple are expanding their farming operations. They are interested in the changes this bill may provide. Unlike many rural areas, I have a couple of Hutterite colonies who have expressed their concern about the Farm Credit Corporation.
I welcome this opportunity to speak. My colleagues, the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) and the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Sargeant) stated that in some ways the bill does not present the solution because it does not look at the real problems farmers face today.
There is no over-all agricultural or transportation policy which the Liberals are following at this time that this FCC bill can fit into. It is interesting to note with regard to transportation that in today's Globe and Mail, it is reported that Saskatchewan Liberals under the leadership of Ralph Goodale are starting to make noises about coming out in favour of the Crowsnest Pass agreement. They know if they stick with what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is trying to abolish, they will not survive a provincial election in Saskatchewan.
The government is not dealing with some of the over-all, basic problems in this FCC bill. One point underlined earlier by the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre is so poignant to this issue that I should emphasize it. On January 28, the hon. member stated:
This particular bill, this move to attempt to free up more funds through the Farm Credit Corporation, will assist; but I hope that the government and the minister will focus more attention on doing something about the real problem, the farm income problem, and will get on with programs for improved marketing and better stabilization which will bring us better net farm incomes.
My constituents involved in farming know that costs have gone up considerably over the past number of years. Input costs have grown. At the same time the amount of money they
February 2, 1982

receive has been decreasing. They are caught in the cost-price squeeze. As a result many are forced to apply to the FCC. They need credit in order to maintain a viable farming operation. If the government was following a food policy and if the farmers were getting a fair return, there would be no need to worry about farm credit.
It is interesting to note from statistics that interest rates have become the number one cost for farmers. According to the projected figures for 1981, farmers will be faced with interest on indebtedness to the tune of $2,168 billion. That is a huge amount that the farmers of Canada are being forced to absorb as part of their operation. In my province, the projected figure spent by farmers on interest for 1981 is $201.9 million. This problem is faced by the farmers in my constituency. I am glad to see that there will be some loosening up on the part of the government with regard to the Farm Credit Corporation.
When we examine the whole matter of credit and how financial institutions are involved in farm credit, it is rather interesting to see how the minister over the years has been singing a different song. As early as October 25, 1977, when the minister was speaking to the Canadian Bankers' Association at the fifth agricultural credit conference at the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa, he was taking off his hat-I suppose it was that green hat the minister wears even when he comes to my constituency-and saying: "I take off my hat to the banks and other interested financial organizations who are starting to get involved in long-term agricultural lending programs, because I welcome progress and this is progress." 1 see that he has obviously been walking on the road to Damascus, because in his speech on January 28 he does bring in a more realistic view of banks. I am happy to see that he is putting his finger on where part of the problem lies.

To then give the banks an increased share of long-term credit is very

inconsistent to me. It is no wonder that I have been faced by a number of constituents who have complained that they cannot get Farm Credit Corporation loans. This is because the proportion of help that has been given by the FCC has been declining rapidly over the last five years.
If we want to have a stable food supply and ensure that farmers stay in production, they must be provided with the opportunity to borrow money at a rate which allows them to stay in business. As my colleagues have pointed out and as I suggest again to the minister, he should take heed of what organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has said with regard to interest rates. He was referring to the fact that the loans of the Farm Credit Corporation would now be 16.75 per cent because the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had not been able to convince cabinet to retain the loans at 14 per cent. I wish the minister had been more authoritative and able to do more arm twisting of his cabinet colleagues to impress upon them the importance of our entire agricultural sector.
In the amendments brought about by Bill C-88, the minister mentions new sources of future funding, the fact that this bill would enable the FCC to borrow in the financial markets. He introduces a measure which would enable retiring farmers to contribute to a pool which would have additional funding for the FCC. Again, this bill is not specific and the minister should have talked to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) before he brought down his budget on November 12, so that perhaps the income-averaging annuity contracts could have been replaced by a measure such as this and farmers who were retiring might have been able to contribute toward the self-sufficiency of farming by contributing some of their own retirement savings plans under this proposal that the minister has been underlining.
We welcome some of the loosening up we see in these new amendments because of the higher costs of machinery and the higher costs of building. We welcome the fact that applicants will benefit from the higher upper limits on amounts which can be borrowed. It is interesting that this bill provides maximum amounts of loans which will henceforth be prescribed by regulation rather than statute. It is good that the minister has proposed an increase for people who are single farmer applicants from a maximum limit of $200,000 to $300,000; and for more than one applicant the upward limit on Farm Credit Corporation loans is increased from $400,000 to $500,000. It is good that we are moving in the direction of recognizing the increased costs farmers are forced to pay.
I am also very pleased that under these Farm Credit Corporation amendments there will be some authority to disburse up to 30 per cent of a loan based on acceptable security while registration of a mortgage and other security arrangements are
being made. This should prove somewhat helpful to farmers who will be borrowing from the Farm Credit Corporation.
It is also good to see that the age limit for people borrowing money from the Farm Credit Corporation is being deleted. I must commend the work done by my colleague the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake in applying pressure on the government to remove the age limit. The age limit for borrowing was 35 and under. People will now be allowed to work off the land for up to five years before engaging in full-time farming, if that is their situation. I know the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake outlined some of the things he did in relation to appealing to the Human Rights Commission to see that this age discrimination at the Farm Credit Corporation ceased. I am very happy to see this being done. In my constituency there have been people who have wanted to borrow money from the Farm Credit Corporation, but they have not found the Farm Credit Corporation to be as helpful as they would have liked.
When we are dealing with this Farm Credit Corporation bill later on in committee, I hope we will be able to bring in even better amendments which would assist farmers. While we are doing this I hope we will also remember that we must deal with the basic problem farmers are facing in all our rural constituencies, and that is the problem of farm net income. While necessary, in some ways the credit measures we are looking at are not the real solution to the problems farmers are facing. So I urge the government to take a closer look at some of the basic problems of farmers in relation to stabilization and marketing so that the farmer might continue to play a vital role in our Canadian economy and be able to continue farming and provide us with the food supplies we need.
Those are some of my concerns relating to Bill C-88 as it is before us at the present time.

The riding of Levis, which I have been proudly representing since May 4 of last year, consists largely of farmers, especially in the southern part of the riding which includes farms that are the envy of many farmers in Quebec. I am very pleased to be able to discuss this bill, especially since Canadian and Quebec farmers have been seriously affected by the economic situation during the past months and weeks, just like industry and business. First, I should like to refer to the throne speech of April 14, 1980, and I quote:
Food and agriculture are going to be increasingly important to the Canadian economy in the 1980s. To further strengthen the industry, my government plans to create a Canadian Agricultural Export Corporation to expand markets for Canadian producers. A meat import act will be introduced to protect both consumers and producers.
The present government has indeed kept the promises made in the throne speech from which I have just quoted. In fact,

the legislation on meat imports was passed by the House on December 11, 1981.
As for the Canadian Agricultural Exports Corporation known as Canagrex, the bill is now before the House and it should not take more than a few days before the corporation is established. Canagrex will very substantially serve the interests of Canadian farmers by helping them discover and expand important export markets for Canadian agricultural products. In his budget speech on November 12, 1981, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) announced special measures to help farmers who are unable to keep their business going because of the present interest rates. These farmers will be able to obtain loans at a rate of 11.75 per cent, which is 5 per cent less than the usual rate charged by the Farm Credit Corporation. The minister also announced that $50 million would go to the FCC to finance additional loans and reduce interest rates for our Canadian and Quebec farmers. The minister also said that farmers would now be eligible for the Small Business Development Bond program. However, our farmers need more assistance than these measures are able to provide, and that is why today the House is debating legislation that will make the Farm Credit Corporation more accessible to farmers. Perhaps a few statistics would be useful concerning the Farm Credit Corporation or at least some figures on agriculture in Quebec. Six per cent of Canadian farmland is located in Quebec, and 13.5 per cent of farm income is earned by Quebecers. The fact that 20 per cent to 23 per cent of the total budget of Agriculture Canada, including the Dairy Commission, is spent in Quebec is ample proof of the Canadian presence in Quebec agriculture. This is according to figures published late in 1980. In dollars and cents, it is about $160 million per year. I think it is always useful to have a few figures on hand, because there are always people who claim the Government of Canada, the present Liberal government, is doing absolutely nothing for agriculture in Quebec. Now I think that quite the opposite is true and that those statistics show it beyond doubt.
1 also noted that several members opposite have supported the substance of the bill now under consideration. I am, therefore, pleased to agree with them. With respect to this bill, I would like to point out some interesting new provisions, knowing that the Farm Credit Corporation was set up 22 years ago and that it has lent over $5 billion to some 160,000 Canadian farmers including a great majority of Quebecers. Almost 74,000 loans are now in effect, of which 4,328 have been granted during the financial year 1981-82. In mid-January of the current financial year, the total amount lent to farmers reached $426.9 million with average costs largely exceeding $98,000. One of the important amendments proposed is to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to seek other Financing sources than strictly government sources. In fact, this means that the Farm Credit Corporation will be able to

borrow on independent financial markets instead of always having to beg from the government.
Another very important change proposed in this bill is that the ceiling for loans will now be set by regulation instead of being provided in the act, which prevents the minister from having to introduce a new bill each time the loan limit has to be changed. In view of the lengthy procedure which must be followed to amend legislation, I believe it will be to the advantage of Canadian and Quebec farmers if the act allows our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who is doing an exceptional job, to proceed by regulation instead of waiting weeks and months before being able to introduce a bill.

ration, I mean the Farm Credit Corporation, has made available over 60 per cent of all the long-term farm credit over the past few years. The rest was made available through provincial organizations, banking institutions, credit unions, caisses populates and private lenders.
Since 1973, the funds available for long-term farm credit have been increasing by as much as 20 per cent every year. It increased from $655 million in 1975 to $1.9 billion in 1980, and it is expected to keep on increasing. It becomes, therefore, more and more urgent to provide the Farm Credit Corporation with an adequate and stable source of funds. The FCC's role has always been to help young farmers and, in fact, the majority of approved loans have gone to farmers under 35, whose share has remained relatively constant at 70 per cent during the last three years. Up to now, loans were mainly used to purchase additional land or new farming units. However, the number of loans granted to consolidate debts has increased significantly because of the spectacular rise in interest rates. The percentage of such loans rose from 24.8 per cent on March 31, 1980, to 27.1 per cent on September 30, 1981. On this subject I should like to quote Mr. Marcel Mailloux of the Farm Producers' Union in an article published in La Terre de chez nous of December 10, 1981. I prefer to quote Mr. Mailloux directly to let him make this point:
When we met here last year, the bank rate was 12.8 per cent. Six months later, it was over 21 per cent, at a level no one would have believed possible a year ago.
The extremely high level of interest rates during the past year has had and continues to have a serious impact on many farming operations. In 1980, Quebec farmers paid $154 million in interest to various financial institutions, their second largest expenditure after feed purchases.
Why do farmers have such large interest payments? The reason is simple and you know it as well as I do: Interest payments reflect the increasing productivity of our agricultural industry.
From Mr. Mailloux's words it is clear that one of the industry's main problems-and it shares this with other sectors-is interest rates. Although we have excellent legislation providing for access to credit, until we make it possible for farmers to repay their loans, they will move steadily closer to bankruptcy. I feel it would be useful to set up a special program to help Canadian farmers by, for instance-and there often have been recommendations to that effect-setting a ceiling of, let us say, 40 per cent on interest rates for Canadian farmers. Naturally, farmers would benefit from any drop in interest rates on the same grounds as people in business or industry.
According to a study made by Mrs. Louise St-Pierre, agricultural producers have taken a different approach to financing, allegedly because many of them were facing new problems created by soaring interest rates which forced them to refinance their debts over longer terms. compared with an estimated value of $15.10 billion in 1979. This information is contained in a report published by the Farm Credit Corporation Research Division.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude by saying that I will gladly support the bill now before the House, assured as I am that this measure is only one step on the part of the Liberal government in its effort to provide further assistance to Canadian farmers. In light of the recent statistics and the results achieved after 15 or 20 consecutive years of Liberal administration, there is no doubt whatsoever that the farming community will be ever better served by this government. I hope that all spokesmen for the agricultural sector, whether they belong to the provincial government, the Agricultural Producers' Union or the farming community, will work hand in hand with the federal government, because I am sure that is the road to success. I would suggest that no one stands to gain anything by attacking, threatening or insulting the various levels of government, and I remain convinced that we can rightfully expect that co-operation will stand the agricultural community in good stead.

I can assure this House, however, that we are not talking about the kind of nuts produced in other parts of Canada; I am talking about the kind of nuts we eat. This bill is very important to the people of Okanagan North and to all Canadians. I am very glad to see that with this bill and with the Canagrex legislation, which will be discussed tomorrow, the government has finally started something positive. I would be the first to commend the government for doing that. The minister has said in bringing this bill before the House that Canadian agriculture must be assured of a constant and sufficient supply of long-term credit if it is to meet the goals set for its agri-food strategy.
I have looked far and wide for any strategy, and I mean good strategy from this government in the agricultural industry, whether its produce is for home use or export. I will have something more to say about that later on. The bill itself is positive. It seeks to encourage and assist the production of agriculture. Together with Canagrex, this bill will help to rationalize the export of food from this country. It broadens the scope of the Farm Credit Corporation. Capital is increased from $150 million to $225 million, which given the 25 times roll-over, allows for about a $5.6 billion line of credit. Furthermore, it allows the corporation to go to the private market. While it is not perfect, I would endorse the comments of the hon. member for Huron-Bruce (Mr. Cardiff)-and I hope this matter will be brought up again in committee-that there should be a regulation that only resident farmers are entitled to borrow money under the act.
The hon. member mentioned foreigners buying land in Canada. I realize that must be controlled at the provincial level but certainly in the Okanagan it is a big problem. We have foreigners paying very high prices for very good land, because it is a nice place to live. However, they do not live on the land; therefore its productivity is down.
Now, I said earlier that this is the first positive thing this government has done in two years. I have sat here for just over two years and seen nothing but negative and punitive legislation. In fact, there was a time when I thought the government's whole purpose was to savage Canadians. First of all, we had the energy crisis and this government's energy policy. All it succeeded in doing was to ruin what at one time was a very good industry in western Canada, Mr. Speaker. The drilling and associated service industry has virtually disappeared because of this government's policies. That really hurt western Canadians.
The second bit of legislation in another direction was also negative. The government made it impossible for most people to communicate by mail because of the high cost of postage. It stopped most of the rail passenger activity in western Canada,

and altogether had a very negative impact on transportation and communications.
The third attack on the country was the too high interest rates. They have affected everyone, and most certainly the farm population. When I was home over the holidays I spent a lot of time talking to farmers and business people, and high interest rates was the main topic of conversation. One farmer in particular said he was in danger of losing his farm. He reminded me of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and asked me to see if it was still in effect. Now, there are perhaps many in this House not old enough to remember the thirties; you might, Mr. Speaker, and I do, but it was a very, very difficult time for farmers, not only because of a lack of markets but because of failed crops, bad weather and dust storms. In fact, we used to call them the dirty thirties.
However, it was the Bennett government at that time, a Conservative government, which brought in an act that made it possible for farmers on the verge of bankruptcy to come to terms with their creditors, and if they could not the courts were empowered to force an agreement on the farmers and their creditors. This farmer said that he saved his land at that time because of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. He has farmed that land for 40 years because of that act; he has been productive, and I am sure his story can be repeated many times in western Canada.
This farmer asked me, why can we not do something like that now? Well, I think that is the kind of forward-looking legislation that this government should be bringing forth. Hopefully they will; hopefully Bill C-88 and the Canagrex bill mark a change in the government's direction. Certainly in the past 15 years it has not shown any real strategy for agriculture. Everyone, Mr. Speaker, who has spoken to this bill has emphasized the need to protect the farming operation because, over the long term, I think most Canadians will agree it is absolutely essential.
I want to talk now about what has happened to Canada in relation to the farming community, agricultural production and exports in general, because both these bills address that question. I read recently an article in the January, 1979 issue of the Chelsea Journal which identified the result of this government's failure to have a national policy of agricultural production and export. It said that as a nation we can produce our own breakfast, but we must send out for lunch and dinner. That is a very apt way of saying we have failed. We can produce only our breakfast; if we want lunch or dinner we have to go outside the country and buy it.
By the year 2000 Canada will be a net importer of every food with the exception of grains, oilseed, milk and eggs. We will be making our breakfast but nothing else. That is a sad commentary on a country which was once a great agricultural producer. The article goes on to say that Canada is an underdeveloped country where agricultural trade is concerned. That was a surprise to me, Mr. Speaker. I had not heard the word "underdeveloped" in relation to Canada for a long, long time.

This article then goes on to prove it. First of all, the pattern of agricultural trade in an underdeveloped country shows certain characteristics. First of all, they specialize only in one or two major exported crops. They mentioned Brazil with coffee at 33 per cent and sugar at 21 per cent of its export trade. Tanzania has 31 per cent of its trade in coffee. The Philippines exports of sugar represent 33 per cent of its total trade. Seventy-eight per cent of the Dominican Republic's trade is in sugar. Does Canada fit this pattern? Of course it does. Forty per cent of our trade is solely in wheat, a raw product.
The article goes on to say that as a result of this fact we are subject to wild fluctuations in export prices. That also marks an underdeveloped country. It points out that Brazil earned $1.1 billion from the sale of sugar in 1975, but only $421 million in 1972. Canada earned $2 billion from the sale of wheat in 1975, but only $687 million in 1970.
Another characteristic of an underdeveloped country is that most of its food is exported in the unprocessed, crude form. As a result, you lose jobs in the processing industry.
Another characteristic is that farmers are forced off the land, mostly by the large agri-business corporations. We have not yet reached Brazil's stage where some 6.3 million farmers have left the land, but we have seen the beginning of the trend. There were 381,000 fewer farmers in Canada in 1976 than in 1951. The farming population is down to 5.1 per cent of the population, compared to 16.8 per cent only a few short years ago.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am perfectly aware that you need an economic unit in order to farm. I have lived in Saskatchewan and have seen where a farmer starved on a quarter section. Later on he starved on a half section, and barely made a living on three quarters of a section a few years later. There are now much larger economic units and I agree with that. There had to be some rationalization of the whole system. But it does not mean that you have to rationalize him out of existence. I think it is a well-known fact that farm land is more productive in the hands of a family farm unit than under any other system. Certainly much more so than the large agri-businesses which are now demanding great quantities of land.
1 was very glad to see that at least Prince Edward Island is attempting to put a stop to this. Some time ago the Irving Corporation wanted to add another 6,000 acres to their existing holdings, which would have given them about 10,000 acres on that small island. The government there indicated that perhaps they will put a limit of 3,000 acres on what any one person or corporation can own. I agree with that; I think farming is essential to our way of life.
Canada is certainly an underdeveloped country in relation to its food exports and is in great danger of using most of its arable land for cash crops. Again, I do not think we will ever become like some countries, such as Brazil or Mexico. As a result of large corporations taking a great deal of the land and using it for cash crops, the benefit to the citizens of those
countries does not match the actual return from the sale of cash crops. An article with which I agree states that today in Brazil the sugar workers are provided with less nutrients than were the slaves back in 1880. That is not a good story.
I think the statistics tell the story in Canada. In 1948 crude food exports amounted to 50 per cent of our total food exports. In 1980 our crude production was four fifths of our total food exports. I think that is unreasonable. In this country we are seeing a greater dependency on processed foods, most of which are imported. As a result, the number of jobs we have lost has become a national scandal. We now have a deficit in 11 of the 12 major fabricated food groups, when as late as 1967 the majority were in a trade surplus position.
In my own constituency we have a good example of what has happened in Canada. At one time we grew and processed tomatoes. Our production of canned tomatoes and ketchup was a very viable business. Today, not one single can of tomatoes or one bit of tomato ketchup is being produced in the Okanagan Valley. That is true of many articles. We are told that if this process continues, the tomato industry in Canada will eventually suffer a loss of some 2,365 jobs. It would not be so bad if the tomatoes imported from these large corporations in the United States and Mexico were any good, but they are designed to be picked up by machinery and not to be eaten. Most of these tomatoes could be used in baseball games and they would not suffer at all.
I think that if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has a strategy, he had better look to that problem very quickly, because we certainly have the wherewithal and the means in this country to produce the kinds of foods we need. It is entirely up to us. to this government and to future governments, because this government has only a couple of years more in which to do anything. First of all, what the government must do is to ensure a self-reliant food industry. Canadian farmers and workers should grow and process food in Canada which is of the required quantity and quality. That is the first step. Second, we should ensure that our workers and farmers have sufficient incomes to purchase the food and articles they need. We have the technical know-how. All we need is some direction in policy toward which the people of this country can work, and a commitment toward lowering the interest rates.
At the moment, as a result of the high interest rate policy, all the capital formation in farming has gone to the United States. And why should it not? We are told that because of this government's policy, 25 per cent of foreign investment in the United States comes from Canada. I think it is a shame when we have the technical know-how. All we need is some financial encouragement, and I hope that it will be forthcoming from the government. As I said earlier, the government is beginning to show signs of some enlightenment. I hope it will continue with this positive attitude and work toward an ever-increasing and productive farm industry.

One of the things the minister knows well, and 1 think it is evident to all of us, particularly from comments made by all opposition parties, is that the farm community is now in a cost-price squeeze. It is in a vice which has been grabbing and squeezing it to death. It is something which can be approached from many sides, although there are some critical factors. The financial arrangements through which farmers must work comprise one of those critical factors.
1 have recently finished a survey in my constituency. We sent out approximately 1,300 questionnaires at almost the same time the Minister of Agriculture sent out questionnaires. We did this, first of all, to ensure that our area was properly understood in the context of this broader survey, because we face some special problems. I will return to that survey in a few moments, after I refer to the changes which will be made to the Farm Credit Corporation.
I would like to make reference to the capital formation of the Farm Credit Corporation. One of the things which seems unclear among the proposed changes is exactly what will happen within that capital formation part. At this point in time we know that we have a capital limit of $150 million. We know that if the request for an additional $14 million were to be granted this year, we will have gone over that limit. We are now at $143 million, and this bill would change the upper limit of capital to $225 million. The trick is that the Farm Credit Corporation can loan 25 times the amount of its capital. The Farm Credit Corporation is requesting that the government consider giving it $14 million. If one multiplies that by 25, that will mean a $350 million increase in the borrowing capacity of the Farm Credit Corporation this year. That is clearly inadequate to meet the needs of agriculture right now, and it is something which should certainly be expanded by several millions of dollars at the capital side. I know the minister knows that, and that is something we need in a hurry if we are to address the problems presently sitting in the agricultural community.
The other side to that capital formation is that the 25 factor could also be changed, so that instead of only providing another $14 million times 25, equalling $350 million, the factor could be changed, for instance, to 30 times the capital, allowing an expansion of borrowing capacity to the Farm Credit Corporation which would directly address most of the requirements of agriculture. That would work well, and there is no reason why it cannot be done.

We must also consider the source of this borrowed money. The minister has suggested that the Farm Credit Corporation could borrow from sources other than the government in order to satisfy its requirements. One of the dangers, of course, that this bill has presented is that if the total borrowing limits are still the same, we will not really have accomplished a heck of a lot. If the government reduces its commitment and allows the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow from other sources, then the government will be off the hook as far as providing funds is concerned. However, we will really not have done anything to increase the amount of available capital within the Farm Credit Corporation. Therefore, what we really want to ensure is that the government maintains its commitment while allowing expansion of capital from private sources, if possible.
We must ensure that interest rates applying to funds borrowed from private sources are not too high. It is a good idea and should be promoted vigorously. I hope we get a chance to discuss this in committee.

those areas where there are a few options, at least in the short term, for those involved in the red meat industry.
In the survey we have just finished compiling, 1,600 questionnaires were sent out. There were 473 people who responded. We found that 10.1 per cent of all farmers have their farms for sale-and this is dairy and all types of agricultural industries-in the whole of Bruce County. The important point is that in the red meat industry, those who have any type of beef or pork, an additional 30 per cent are considering selling their farms. That says something for the industry.

The critical factor is that the extra $50 million available for farm credit will not solve the problem. It helps in areas where the FCC feels it can make a loan because there is a viable operation. It will obviously only help for a year or two, will be reviewed, and there will again be the same problem. It looks at one area incompletely, but at least it is addressing it.
There is another area which, as the minister knows, has been discussed in a number of forums in the past several months. This is the area where people are now without equity. They could be called technically bankrupt. They are in a situation which continues to deteriorate. There is no answer. Some of these people might be criticized for being poor managers.
In his speech, the minister indicated his understanding of the fact that there needed to be a certain size operation in order to be competitive and productive in a way that the farmer could earn a living. The farm size grew as people were expanding their operation. They were doing things right, but they were caught in a squeeze because of changes in energy prices. A lot of farmers were concerned about that when the Conservative Party was in power. They are caught just as badly now, if not worse. They will have to spend $4.50 an acre more over the next year. All of these things coming together have left these people in a situation which has to be looked at in a serious way.
There have been a number of suggestions. There are three basic solutions to this problem. One is akin to the farmers and creditors act introduced in the thirties. It is something that nobody likes to consider seriously if they do not have to, but it is a humane way of looking at the situation that exists today.
Something else that has been suggested with some historic precedent, as far as ARDA is concerned and what it does, is a kind of land banking. I read some of the comments about what happened in Saskatchewan. In order to address the problem, some answer that includes land banking and government ownership in the land for at least an interim period might be considered.
Finally, what could be considered, and would not be an awful lot different in terms of legislation or the way the minister and his department look at the situation, would be an
instance where a farmer was able to negotiate a settlement on his own behalf with a particular financial institution, and that institution writes off some of the amount. I know of one case where the bank is prepared to write off $800,000. In spite of the fact this person has been a good manager and is respected in the community, he is in a situation now where he cannot go anywhere else to raise the money to resolve the situation. He cannot get the kind of support that would give confidence to another financial institution. The same financial institution that would negotiate the settlement is clearly not in the position where it wants to refinance this man. Therefore, that kind of negotiation would serve the purposes of the bank. It would certainly serve the purposes of individual farmers involved in this area. It could be supported by the government either through the Farm Credit Corporation or by government guarantees, either with or without the co-operation of the provincial government. It could answer one of the last problems remaining to be solved.
We are working through some of these matters, including marketing, which the minister knows is important, the longer-term financing of lower rates that he knows is important, and the rationalization of the whole red meat industry and whether that will be a specialty product in the future.
Others have mentioned many other points; I will not go into them. I look forward to speaking at committee stage of this bill in an attempt to understand what the minister has in mind. We know that the regulatory aspects of this bill have been expanded. I find it confusing when I read some of the minister's remarks in years gone by with regard to the amount of discretionary power which civil servants have and now see him giving them more power. I guess there is good news and bad news about that. If it speeds up the process and avoids legislative delay, that is good. However, I wonder whether he is going to change his mind about some of those things we talked about before.
I end my remarks with the hope that the minister will address that one area in agriculture that has been missed, to the detriment of the individual farmer who deserves his integrity and degree of dignity as he is trying to go through a painful readjustment, but one which will serve well the interests of the minister, his department and all Canadians.

Loans were traditionally made to farmers for one purpose, the purchase of land, buildings and machinery. That was the largest amount, not only in dollar value but in the number of loans that were made. Although this still applies today, there is a new component. It is a feature which we have begun using, and that is line of credit. Today farmers not only have mortgages, they must go to financial institutions to obtain an additional line of credit in order to operate. In other words, they must pay the mortgage and machinery costs as well as pay that line of credit. This line of credit generally runs from year to year and is settled before the next crop year starts. With lower farm incomes and higher interest rates, the ability to pay that line of credit becomes very difficult for farmers.
My hon. friend from Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin), who has just finished speaking, has many constituents engaged in the operation of feed lots and who operate on a yearly basis. They obtain a loan as a line of credit in order to finish cattle for sale at the end of the year. Then they pay back their line of credit with the hope of having some money left over to clothe themselves and pay off their mortgage. That is how farming operates today.
One day during the Christmas break-it was about minus 31 on one of our more balmy days in Manitoba this winter-1 was driving down the highway listening to the CBC farm report on the radio. Mr. Speaker, that budget was not taxation; that budget was confiscation. There is a big difference. We all
criticize taxation and argue about the rate because none of us wants to pay tax. There is quite a difference between payment of taxes, however, and the confiscation of property on which taxes have been paid over the years. TThere is a great difference.
As I remember the constitutional debate, if I feel any chagrin it is about property rights. In one way or another the idea of property rights-that a person may own something after he or she has worked for it-is being eroded. It is being chipped away; it is being chiselled away.
I am sure many other members have had the experience of people coming to them with this question: "Why is it, when I want to retire, the government insists on taxing me first when I have worked all these years in order that I might live in dignity in the sunset years of my life?" That question is not being answered by the Minister of Finance or by the Minister of Agriculture.
I should like to say something about the administration of the FCC. I notice that there are some officials in the gallery who I presume are from FCC, and I think it is important that they understand what we hear about the administration. I must say that in general terms I think it is valuable and that I think the administration is excellent. The officials are often confronted by people who are in difficulty, people who need a loan and obviously the need has to be assessed in a very rational way. But I want to tell them that farmers do not come to them in a master-servant relationship. Perhaps there is a defence mechanism involved on the part of officials of the FCC but we often hear the complaint from farmers that they feel it is due to the good graces of the person across the desk that they receive the loan. That person's job is one of administration, not to make that Canadian farmer feel that if he gets anything he should be very thankful to the person sitting across the desk.
In the whole question of administration the Catch 22 situation arises time after time. A young farmer comes into the FCC looking for a loan. He is told that he can obtain a loan if he has enough equity, and the farmer says, "My dear friend, I would not be here if I had the equity; I could go to a different financial institution." Very often banks are willing to take risks on the potential of a young farmer, on the potential of his land, on the potential of his management ability, or on the potential of his willingness and that of his wife and family to work. Often banks and credit unions are much more willing to take a risk than the FCC.
Another matter of administration was brought to my attention recently. I do not know how it will be resolved, but I have written to the minister in the past few days about it. I am referring to the situation where a farmer obtains a loan and goes into a local place of business, such as a lumberyard or a farm supply dealer, and shows his line of credit. He says that he wants to build a facility or a barn with the proceeds of his loan. He starts building his barn and because there is a line of credit through the FCC, the supplier advances the materials.

But suddenly the barn is not quite complete and FCC demands that it be completed. Now the supplier is in a Catch 22 situation. He either advances more supplies in order to get his money, because FCC will not advance it to the farmer, or he stops the project right there. I know a lumber dealer who advanced materials and $7,000 is outstanding, but the person who received the FCC loan left the province-he walked away, so to speak. Obviously the FCC has the first mortgage, and in order to protect himself, the lumber dealer took a second mortgage on which I do not think he will ever realize any return. Not only does FCC have a responsibility to farmers, it must modernize its administrative system, particularly concerning the manner in which supplies are received and building materials are purchased by some people with FCC loans.
If there is hope in the country, I believe there is hope because of agriculture. I have been somewhat critical of the minister today because the farmers with whom I have spoken have been extremely critical of the minister over the last few months. What they have been saying is: "Would you tell them in the House of Commons that first there must be a recognition, not in words but in action, that agriculture is extremely important for Canada's future." Perhaps that sounds prosaic, that everyone understands and agrees with it, but this is not so.
Today we hear much about an industrial strategy, which is valid and important, but the development of farming and a method of meeting the problems and challenges of farming should be as much a part of the industrial strategy as rebuilding, for instance, industries in central Canada to make them more competitive. When there is a lay-off in farming, it affects a farmer, his wife and his family and their future and dreams. When someone who works for Massey-Ferguson is laid off, we hear about the numbers. Both are tragic, but there must be a recognition that farming is important. We should not only give it lip service. It must become part of the national strategy. Also we must do a better job of selling. Today I often hear the word "marketing". 1 am not against marketing boards, but I want to see hard-nosed people out in the marketplace selling Canadian agricultural products. We are not doing an adequate job in that regard.
1 should like to refer to the example of the first shipments of canola to Japan. Yes, the Canadian government was interested but it did not know what to do. I know a farmer who said, "Look, 1 will do it". He filled containers and said that he would clean it in Canada. The Japanese had a certain standard, they thought it could only be done in Japan. When the farmer delivered the canola to Japan, cleaned in Canada, it had a lower dockage rate than the best cleaning facilities in Japan. This is what Canadian farmers are capable of doing. We must get out there and sell.
1 should like to refer to another example in the time remaining; that is, the Canadian Egg Marketing Agency. Over 50 per cent of all eggs produced in Manitoba are produced by a number of farmers in my riding. Over the last few weeks I have been trying to obtain, through CEMA, permission to purchase eggs through an international contact in excess of
11,000	cases per week. The average farmer produces 100 cases
Farm Loans
per week, so one can imagine how much I am talking about. I cannot obtain that. I have talked with farmers in British Columbia and in Manitoba, and they have said, "Give us the opportunity and we will produce those eggs." When marketing becomes more important than selling, we run into trouble. This is what has happened.
I am for marketing. We need good marketing, but we also need hard-nosed selling. We also must be able to assure Canadian farmers that they will retain their assets. If we do not assure young Canadians who want to become involved in farming that the assets will be theirs first, that they will be their pension plans, that the Government of Canada will not confiscate through capital gains and change the rules in the middle, as we saw with the budget, we will not attract young Canadians into farming.
Those of us who grew up on farms-and perhaps tragically were not able to continue that life-say that farming has a great future, but we must allow farmers to do what they do best-farm. We should not interfere, but we should encourage.
